transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-29
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Ruiz (Neptune ML), Leah O'Connor (Neptune Infra), Samir Patel (Neptune Data)
Notes: benchmark sheet referenced (https://docs.company/benchmark-neptune), security pack link (https://secure/redwood/security/neptune)

[00:00] Jordan (AE): okay great, thanks everyone for taking time. quick check, audio okay?
[00:22] Mark: yep, good here. thanks for scheduling. we wanted to use this time to figure out the quantization regressions we've hit and whether a hybrid strategy makes sense for our VPC pilot.
[01:10] Jordan: perfect. high level agenda — Priya will walk through the runtime tradeoffs for INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ; then we'll map that to KV warmup and batching behavior; last we'll scope the VPC/onprem pilot and rollout plan. sound good?
[01:45] Leah: yes, and we also want to understand what causes the accuracy drops we saw after converting to GPTQ — specifics per-layer would help.
[02:20] Priya (SE): cool. quick context recap from what you sent — model is a 30B instruction-tuned variant, typical sequence length 600 tokens, prefix-heavy prompts for summarization, very spiky arrival patterns. workload wants p95 latency under 500ms for short completions, and throughput cost sensitivity. correct?
[03:05] Mark: that's right. latency SLA is soft for batch jobs, but for interactive parts we need the 500ms target. also KV cache is important because most requests are continued sessions.
[03:40] Priya: got it. first: quant families quick primer (and I'll be rough here cause of time). INT8 (linear symmetric / per-channel) gives best memory reduction but sometimes hurts activation dynamics in attention layers — leads to hallucination-like shifts. FP8 (recent microformats) tends to retain dynamic range for softmax and attention but has hardware availability limits. GPTQ and AWQ are post-training quantization pipelines — GPTQ optimizes per-weight with Hessian-ish approximations; AWQ includes activation-aware calibration and often better controls bias but more infra to run.
[04:45] Samir: we ran GPTQ and saw a 7% macro-f1 drop on our validation prompts, primarily in factual recall. is that consistent with what you see?
[05:14] Priya: yes, that's plausible — recall errors tend to come from quantization noise in the final MLP layers and output heads. GPTQ can sometimes produce that if calibration sets didn't cover long-tail prompts. AWQ often helps but can still fail if KV cache warmup changes hidden state trajectories.
[05:45] Jordan: important nuance: in our runtime, mixing precisions layerwise (e.g., keep last 2 MLPs FP16/FP32 and rest INT8/AWQ) is a common mitigation. that reduces cost while preserving quality. we call this a precision-blend or layerwise mix.
[06:25] Leah: we tried layerwise mixing but saw latency jitter — our onprem setup has variable NUMA and bandwidth. is that expected?
[06:50] Priya: yes, mixing precisions can change kernel selection and memory footprints which affects batching and KV cache warmup. on certain GPUs the kernel for FP16 matmuls is different path than INT8, so switching mid-graph can add synchronization points, slightly nudging p95. this is why profiling on your exact infra is critical.
[07:30] Mark: that ties into KV behavior — we noticed when cache is cold, responses were fine, but after about 3–4 tokens in a session we started to diverge compared to baseline. could that be staleness or rounding accumulation?
[08:05] Priya: two separate, but related things: (1) KV warmup mismatch — if quantized KV scale is different, early tokens use a different distribution; (2) accumulation / rounding noise across many recurrences can bias hidden states. We often see divergence in prefix-heavy sessions where the cached keys/values were produced under different precision.
[08:45] Samir: is that an artifact of continuous batching? we batch prefixes across requests in Redwood runtime, right? could batch mixing cause this?
[09:10] Priya: yes, continuous batching can interleave requests with varying sequence lengths; if batches mix warm/cold states created with different precision variants, you can see cross-request contamination at the microsecond level. our runtime has isolation heuristics to avoid mixing in-flight KV buffers across incompatible model-variants; but if you run multiple model-variants behind a single route (e.g., INT8 vs AWQ) and the runtime auto-falls back, you'll get tricky interactions.
[10:00] Jordan: for Neptune's case, we recommended initially pinning a model variant per route for the pilot to avoid mixing. then perform controlled canaries with small traffic percentages.
[10:35] Leah: about pinning — in our VPC pilot we want to test Dedicated vs Private (VPC-hosted) — any differences in warmup behavior we should be aware of?
[11:00] Priya: the underlying runtime is the same, but networking and cold-start patterns differ. Dedicated runs in Redwood-managed infra with stable NUMA/placement, so kernel selection is predictable. Private VPC (customer infra) can have more variance — e.g., pinned GPUs might have different SM occupancy. That's where we saw the jitter you mentioned. Also KMS/HSM calls during startup (for key retrieval) can add latency spikes if not cached.
[11:45] Mark: KMS overhead — we encrypt embeddings at rest and rotate keys — does Redwood support KMS on the critical path or offload?
[12:05] Jordan: we support both: synchronous KMS on startup, and optional cached wrapping for per-token operations. for VPC we recommend cached unwrap on node boot, with audit logs forwarded to your SIEM. we'll include recommended KMS patterns in the security pack.
[12:35] Samir: back to quant algorithms — if we run AWQ vs GPTQ, how do we compare deployment complexity and rollback options?
[12:55] Priya: GPTQ often has smaller conversion infra but less activation calibration; AWQ has a calibration step that tracks activations so it's heavier to run but easier to predict failure modes. For rollback: best practice is dual-bucket deployment — keep FP16 baseline and a quant variant; the runtime can auto-fallback per-request based on SLO breaches. But again if you mix both in same route without isolation you risk KV mismatch.
[13:50] Leah: interesting — so fallback per-request could be dangerous?
[14:05] Priya: it can be if the fallback isn't isolated. We recommend fallback at route-level with prefix affinity: i.e., a session that started on variant A should continue on A or be fully restarted on B after state reset. We have tooling to enforce affinity and to handle graceful restarts with minimal user-visible regression.
[14:45] Mark: how granular are the logs? can we detect when a session switched variants?
[15:10] Jordan: yes, console traces token-level model variant metadata. we'll share an example trace later.
[15:28] Samir: anecdote — when we profiled GPTQ, the final softmax outputs shifted for rare tokens; would layerwise full-precision on the head fix that?
[15:50] Priya: often yes. keeping the final projection and last feed-forward in higher precision re-centers logits. But sometimes earlier attention layers also matter for long-range dependencies. We prioritize last MLP + decoder head first; if problems persist, we escalate layerwise to keep attention Q/K/V in higher precision.
[16:40] Leah: does that change memory footprint significantly? our 30B fits right at the limit.
[16:58] Priya: it's additive — keeping 2–3 layers FP16 may add a few hundred MBs, but usually still much smaller than full FP16 baseline if rest is INT8. We'll give an estimate for your model on your target GPU type.
[17:30] Jordan: next topic: KV cache staleness and coalescing. Priya, can you explain the KV shelf/warmup interaction?
[17:50] Priya: sure. when you have persistent sessions, KV entries stay hot. Quantized KV entries have less numeric fidelity; if a session was cached under FP16 and later read under INT8, the mismatch can be large. Also KV shelf policies (how long cache entries are kept) interact with autoscaling; if nodes evict keys frequently, you get more cold-starts and more potential divergence. We recommend two mitigations: consistent variant per affinity group; and periodic re-warm using a warmup prefix generator to prime the cache with quantized values before real user traffic.
[18:45] Mark: warmup prefix generator — operationally how heavy is that?
[19:05] Priya: light — it's a small synthetic workload that replays typical prefixes for active sessions at low RPS during low-traffic windows. For Neptune's usage pattern we estimated ~2–5% added token cost to keep key occupancy stable.
[19:40] Samir: if we do canary rollouts, should we warm the canary separately?
[19:55] Priya: yes. canary nodes should be pre-warmed with sampled traffic — do not route cold traffic directly. Otherwise you'll see early divergence signals that are false-positives.
[20:20] Leah: ok, let's talk fallbacks and orchestration — you mentioned runtime can enforce affinity, but in VPC can we integrate with our orchestrator (we use Nomad) to prefer certain node pools?
[20:45] Jordan: we can integrate — for Private we expose placement tags and autoscaler hooks that let you target specific node pools for quant variants. Priya will follow up with the deployment playbook for Nomad.
[21:15] Priya: I'll add Nomad example autoscaler rules and the pod/node labels we respect. Also include an experiment to route 10% traffic to AWQ nodes and hold 90% on FP16 baseline for 48 hours while measuring recall metrics.
[21:45] Mark: measurement — what evals should we run during that 48h?
[22:05] Priya: baseline metrics: macro-F1 on your validation set, top-k token distribution shifts, perplexity, and two custom QA/regression prompts you gave us. Also track p50/p95 latency and kv-hit ratio. We'll provide dashboards.
[22:45] Samir: what's the recommended rollback policy if macro-F1 drops more than 3%?
[23:05] Jordan: automated rollback threshold at 3% drop plus p95 latency increase >10% triggers auto-failover to baseline. We'll script the webhook to your monitoring to flip traffic.
[23:35] Leah: about telemetry — can we ingest Redwood traces into our Splunk?
[23:50] Jordan: yes, we support forwarders and S3 export of token traces. For private we can push CloudWatch/Prometheus style metrics into your stack. we'll include config examples.
[24:15] Mark: curious about one thing — we ran AWQ and GPTQ with the same calibration set; AWQ performed better but still had a specific pattern: number-entity hallucinations on financial prompts. any idea why numbers are the worst?
[24:45] Priya: numbers are sensitive because logits are often tightly distributed; quantization noise can flip ranking for tokens with similar scores. Also if the model uses positionally encoded numeric patterns, rounding noise accumulates. Keep numeric-critical tokens in higher precision or bias-correct the softmax output with small temperature adjustments.
[25:20] Samir: bias-correction sounds risky — can you give an example?
[25:35] Priya: small deterministic post-processing — for numeric fields apply a constrained generation filter or reranker. Redwood supports reranking pipelines so you can run a lightweight FP16 reranker on top of quantized generation for sensitive fields. That costs extra tokens but is targeted.
[26:05] Leah: reranking — does it require exposing raw logits?
[26:20] Priya: not necessarily; we return token-level scores and n-best lists which the reranker can consume. We'll show you the minimal reranker config.
[26:40] Jordan: shifting to pilot scope — timeline ideas: initial lab ablations (week 1), small onprem/VPC pilot with 10% traffic (week 2–3), extended pilot and canary (week 4), decision. can we align for April run weeks?
[27:05] Leah: yes, April 6th start for VPC pilot works pending network config.
[27:28] Jordan: action: Leah share IAM and network ranges by April 1. Priya will run ablation plan and share result by April 2.
[27:50] Samir: technical Q — what's the recommended sample size for ablation? we worry about false positives from small sets.
[28:10] Priya: we suggest stratified sampling across your heavy prefixed prompts (n=500-1k) plus 200 rare edge cases. we'll provide scripts to bootstrap and run locally.
[28:35] Mark: about cost — if we run mixed precision we save about 35–50% on memory, what's typical token cost delta?
[28:55] Jordan: rough ballpark — INT8 variant can reduce per-token compute cost 30–50% vs FP16 depending on kernel support; AWQ sits between INT8 and FP16 in compute but higher in conversion overhead. We'll generate a more precise estimate for your GPU family.
[29:25] Priya: one more runtime detail: KV coalescing window. by default Redwood uses a 16ms coalescing window for continuous batching; shortening it reduces latency for interactive traffic but lowers batching efficiency. For Neptune's spikey pattern we might shorten the window for hot routes and lengthen for bulk batch jobs.
[30:00] Leah: can that be per-route?
[30:15] Priya: yes, per-route coalescing and batch sizing are configurable in the route policy. We'll include a sample policy for interactive vs batch routes.
[30:45] Mark: regarding regression triage, can you outline a bisect plan if we see a drop in pre-prod during pilot?
[31:10] Priya: rough playbook: 1) reproduce with deterministic seed and same prompt set; 2) run layerwise dequantization (start from last layer) to locate layer sensitivity; 3) test alternative calibration sets; 4) run AWQ with larger activation samples; 5) if still fail, fallback to FP16 for sensitive routes. We'll run a live demo of step 2 in the lab.
[32:00] Samir: how long does step 2 typically take?
[32:20] Priya: depends on model size — for 30B on our lab hardware about 2–6 hours to run dequant checks across key layers if you have precompiled kernels. Conversion steps longer if you need to recompile kernels.
[32:50] Leah: compilation time — can we reuse kernels across nodes?
[33:05] Priya: yes, compiled kernels are cached and can be shared; but ABI differences across GPU driver versions matter. We'll check your driver versions in pre-flight.
[33:35] Jordan: anything else on regressions?
[33:45] Mark: one last ask — can Redwood's Optimize suggest layerwise candidates automatically?
[33:58] Priya: yes, Optimize will recommend quantization profiles by workload; for Private we can run Optimize offline on your sample corpus and return a recommended blend. that's part of the pilot add-on.
[34:20] Jordan: okay let's recap next steps quickly.
[34:35] Priya: recap: 1) Priya to deliver layerwise ablation scripts + dashboard by 2026-04-02; 2) Jordan to send pilot template and pricing for Dedicated vs Private by 2026-04-03; 3) Leah to share VPC network/IAM details by 2026-04-01; 4) Plan VPC pilot start 2026-04-06; 5) Redwood to provide warmup generator and canary config.
[35:20] Leah: sounds good. one operational question — if we detect small steady drift over long sessions (hours), do you have recommended periodic resyncs?
[35:38] Priya: yes, periodic resyncs every N tokens (you choose threshold, e.g., 1024 tokens) that restart session on fresh FK variant or force a short rerank pass. We'll include options.
[35:58] Samir: we also want to capture token-level diffs during canary for forensic — can that be stored off-cluster?
[36:12] Jordan: yes, token traces can be exported to S3 with encryption. retention configurable per route.
[36:35] Mark: ok, any blockers on Redwood side?
[36:45] Jordan: none. we'll need the IAM/network info and a small quota increase for the pilot nodes.
[37:00] Leah: we'll get that over. thanks for the detailed plan.
[37:18] Jordan: great. I'll follow up with calendar invites for the weekly check-ins and link to the shared benchmark sheet.
[37:32] Priya: quick note — we'll include an example ablation result in the shared sheet showing where last MLP dequant caused biggest delta; expect that in 48h.
[37:50] Mark: awesome. one last clarifying Q: when you say "affinity", does that require session sticky load balancing at our LB layer?
[38:05] Priya: either at your LB or our routing layer. For Private, it's easiest to set session cookies at the Redwood side so you don't need to change your LB. We'll show config.
[38:30] Leah: good. thank you.

[38:40] Closing notes:
- Shared artifacts: benchmark sheet + security pack links (above).
- We will run a small demo of layerwise dequantation step 2 in our lab and share output.
- Expect next sync 2026-04-07 (pilot week 1 start)

[39:05] Jordan: thanks everyone. I'll drop the notes and action items into the CRM and the shared folder.
[39:18] Mark: thanks. bye.

(Transcript ends; recording ended at ~15:32 UTC / ~62 minutes elapsed)
